questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting blood for 10 hours. He appears stuporous. Physical examination shows asterixis. His serum ammonium concentration is increased. Endoscopy shows a gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Which of the following processes is most likely to be increased in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Uptake of nitric oxide by microglia

options.label: B
options.html: B. Release of citrulline from neurons

options.label: C
options.html: C. Synthesis of glutamine by the astrocytes

options.label: D
options.html: D. Synthesis of urea by the choroid plexus

options.label: E
options.html: E. Uptake of arginine by neurons

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Educational Objective: When cirrhosis leads to an accumulation of ammonia in the systemic circulation, as seen in this patient, it is converted to glutamine by astrocytes, driving many of the manifestations of hepatic encephalopathy (HE).

Key Concept: Astrocytes are a type of glial cell involved in glutamate homeostasis. Using glutamate transporters, astrocytes remove glutamate from synapses and use glutamine synthetase to metabolize it into glutamine, thereby protecting the brain from glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Ammonia, which accumulates in the body in HE, is also converted to glutamine by this enzyme.

Explanation: In cirrhosis, ammonia builds up in the body because of decreased ammonia metabolism by the liver. This is further exacerbated by portal hypertension as the blood carrying ammonia does not entirely pass through the liver but rather enters directly into the systemic circulation. When ammonia accumulates in the brain, it is metabolized into glutamine by astrocytes, driving many of the manifestations of HE. These neuropsychiatric disturbances range from subtle cognitive defects like impaired attention span and memory deficits to altered mental status and coma. Asterixis, a flapping tremor in which the hands move up and down when the arms are outstretched, is another clinical manifestation of hyperammonemia.

Differential: Cirrhosis can present with edema, ascites, increased bilirubin, jaundice, spider angiomata, and sequelae of portal hypertension such as esophageal varices, hematemesis, splenomegaly, caput medusae, and rectal varices, and HE. In this patient with cirrhosis, ammonia accumulation in the brain most likely led to increased synthesis of glutamine by the astrocytes. Nitric acid, citrulline, and arginine do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of HE, and the choroid plexus does not play a significant role in urea synthesis.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choice A: Uptake of nitric oxide by microglia is incorrect. Microglial cells, derived from precursor monocytes, phagocytose cellular debris and dead neurons. Nitric oxide, a signaling molecule that modulates synaptic plasticity and promotes vasodilation, is involved in the regulation of microglial activity. Nitric oxide is not involved in the pathogenesis of HE.

Choice B: Release of citrulline from neurons is incorrect. When arginine is converted into nitric oxide, citrulline is released as a byproduct of this reaction and exerts its own regulatory effects on acetylcholine signaling. Citrulline is not involved in the pathogenesis of HE.

Choice D: Synthesis of urea by the choroid plexus is incorrect. The choroid plexus regulates the transport and concentration of numerous substances including urea but does not play a significant role in urea synthesis. In cirrhosis, normal mechanisms of detoxification and processing of ammonia via the urea cycle are impaired, and high concentrations of ammonia (and subsequent conversion to glutamine) play a role in the dysfunction of neurons seen in HE.

Choice E: Uptake of arginine by neurons is incorrect. Neurons take up arginine and convert it into nitric oxide and citrulline for use in signaling pathways. Arginine does not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of HE.

questions.stemHtml: A community survey is designed to evaluate residents' opinions about health needs. Each member of the community has the same probability of being selected to be interviewed. Which of the following is the primary purpose of this method of selection?

options.label: E
options.html: E. Improving participation in the survey

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Ensuring all members of the community have the same probability of being selected will result in a sample distribution of members that accurately reflects the community. The ability to generalize the opinions of this sample to the overall population is called generalizability, which is improved by random sampling.

Key Concept: Generalizability of a sample to the population improves with random sampling.

Explanation: Since it is impractical to collect data from every individual in a population, collecting data on a smaller sample of individuals is standard. When the study sample is sufficiently large and the distribution of members of the sample is similar to the population, it is possible to generalize the findings from the study sample to the population. Thus, generalizability (external validity) is contingent on ensuring the sample distribution is similar to the population, which is best achieved by random sampling from the population. Generalizability may also be used in the context of extrapolating the results of one population to another.

Differential: Having a representative sample improves the ability to generalize the sample to the population from which the sample is drawn.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Decreasing measurement bias is incorrect. Measurement bias describes inaccurate collection of data. Inaccurate collection of data is unrelated to random sample selection.

Choice B: Decreasing random error is incorrect. Decreasing random error improves internal validity of the study but does not affect the ability of the sample to be generalized to the population.

Choice C: Decreasing sample size is incorrect. Ensuring participants are chosen randomly does not affect the number of chosen participants. A sufficiently large sample size is required for generalizability.

Choice E: Improving participation in the survey is incorrect. Ensuring participants are chosen randomly would not affect participation in the study.

questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-week history of intermittent fever, chills, headache, joint pain, and leg swelling. She says that the episodes of fever and chills last for 2 to 3 days and then resolve, after which she feels better for a few days. The joint pain is most severe in her wrists and ankles. The pain is most severe in the morning, improves with slow movement, but becomes incapacitating with heavy exercise. She has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. She recently returned from Puerto Rico, where she studied bat populations for 6 months. She appears flushed. Her temperature is 39.4°C (103.0°F), pulse is 87/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a diffuse, erythematous, maculopapular rash over the lower extremities. There is also conjunctival injection, photophobia, and pharyngeal erythema. The wrist and metacarpophalageal joints are tender to palpation and with movement. Complete blood count shows lymphocytopenia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: Chikungunya virus infection causes episodic high fever, inflammatory symmetric polyarthralgia, maculopapular rash, and conjunctival involvement. It is commonly acquired following travel to islands in the Caribbean, such as with this patient.

Evaluation: This patient presents with recurrent febrile episodes accompanied by chills, headache, conjunctival injection, maculopapular rash, and severe symmetric joint pain involving the wrists and ankles. The arthralgias are inflammatory in character, worse in the morning with improvement after gentle movement and marked functional limitation with exertion. Her recent prolonged stay in Puerto Rico, an endemic region for arboviruses, combined with lymphocytopenia and a maculopapular rash, strongly suggests a viral cause transmitted by mosquitoes.

Definition: Chikungunya virus is an alphavirus transmitted by Aedes species mosquitoes that causes an acute febrile illness characterized by high fever, severe symmetric polyarthralgia or arthritis, maculopapular rash, and conjunctivitis. The joint manifestations are often debilitating and typically involve the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, with morning stiffness resembling inflammatory arthritis. Systemic symptoms, such as headache, photophobia, pharyngeal erythema, and lymphocytopenia, are common during the viremic phase. Fever may be intermittent, and although the acute illness is self-limited, joint symptoms can persist for weeks to months because of ongoing immune-mediated inflammation.

Prevention: Prevention relies on avoidance of mosquito exposure through repellents, protective clothing, and vector control in endemic areas.

Treatment: Management is supportive, focusing on antipyretics and NSAIDs for fever and joint pain, as there is no specific antiviral therapy.

Differential: The combination of high fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, and severe inflammatory polyarthralgia after traveling to the Caribbean is most characteristic of chikungunya virus infection and helps distinguish it from other infectious causes such as malaria or Lyme disease, which do not typically produce this symmetric inflammatory arthritis pattern.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Ebola hemorrhagic fever is incorrect. Ebola disease typically presents with severe systemic illness, gastrointestinal symptoms, bleeding diathesis, and high mortality, not intermittent fevers with inflammatory arthritis and rash in a stable outpatient.

Choice C: Histoplasmosis is incorrect. Histoplasmosis is associated with pulmonary symptoms and systemic findings related to fungal dissemination, and it does not cause acute symmetric inflammatory polyarthralgia with rash and conjunctivitis.

Choice D: Lyme disease is incorrect. Lyme disease can cause arthritis, but it is usually monoarticular or oligoarticular involving large joints such as the knee and is associated with erythema migrans rather than a diffuse maculopapular rash and conjunctival injection.

Choice E: Malaria is incorrect. Malaria causes cyclical fevers and systemic symptoms but does not produce prominent inflammatory arthritis, maculopapular rash, or conjunctivitis. Likewise, severe symmetric joint pain is not a defining feature.

questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of heartburn and regurgitation after meals. He also has had occasional shortness of breath after dinner. He says that the symptoms have persisted despite the use of over-the-counter antacids and eating smaller portions of food. He has not had chest pain or other gastrointestinal symptoms. He has never smoked cigarettes or consumed alcoholic beverages. Current medications also include atorvastatin and a multivitamin. He has had no weight loss since his last visit 6 months ago. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. A chest x-ray shows paracardiac opacity and gas bubbles in the right lower thorax. An upper gastrointestinal series with barium swallow shows a smooth compression of the esophagus with displacement to the left and narrowing of the lumen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Paraesophageal hernias are a type of hiatal hernia characterized by the presence of a gastric bubble adjacent to the esophagus on imaging, as in this patient’s case. Patients present with the features and sequelae of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), including chest pain, regurgitation, hoarse voice, chronic cough, and dysphagia. Patients who fail first-line treatment with proton pump inhibitors may require surgical intervention to reinforce the esophageal hiatus and support the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ).

Evaluation: Paraesophageal hernias commonly present with the features and sequelae of GERD, including chest pain, regurgitation, hoarse voice, chronic cough, and dysphagia.

Definition: Hiatal hernias are the abnormal protrusion of the upper gastrointestinal tract through the diaphragmatic esophageal hiatus into the chest. Hiatal hernias can be divided into sliding types, in which the stomach slides up and displaces the GEJ superiorly, and paraesophageal types, in which the GEJ remains in the hiatus and the fundus of the stomach herniates into the thorax alongside it. Both configurations compromise the function of the lower esophageal sphincter, allowing gastric contents to reflux up into the esophagus. Hiatal hernias are diagnosed with endoscopy or with various imaging modalities including x-rays, upper gastrointestinal series with contrast such as barium swallow, and CT scans. These will show a gastric bubble within the mediastinum (often with air-fluid levels) and displacement of the esophagus.

Prevention: Risk factors for paraesophageal hernias include age-related muscle laxity (decreasing the diaphragm’s tone) and increased intra-abdominal pressure from conditions such as chronic coughing or vomiting, obesity, and pregnancy. Weight loss to decrease intra-abdominal pressure can decrease the risk for paraesophageal hernia.

Treatment: First-line treatment is management of associated GERD with proton pump inhibitors. Patients with symptoms refractory to medical treatment (or those with severe sequelae of paraesophageal hernias such as gastric volvulus) may require surgical intervention with a Nissen fundoplication, which fills the hiatus and reinforces the GEJ with the gastric fundus.

Differential: While the other diagnoses listed can present with GERD, the characteristic imaging findings in this patient indicate the presence of a paraesophageal hernia.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Esophageal achalasia is incorrect. Achalasia results from the destruction of neurons in the myenteric plexus, resulting in dysfunctional peristalsis and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. Presenting symptoms include dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and foul breath.

Choice B: Esophageal candidiasis is incorrect. Candidal esophagitis is a known opportunistic infection in an immunocompromised host (eg, chemotherapy, HIV/AIDS). On examination, patients may have oropharyngeal thrush. Evaluation is performed with upper endoscopy, which may show white plaques and mucosal ulcerations, and biopsy, which shows pseudohyphae and budding yeasts.

Choice C: Esophageal diverticulum is incorrect. These outpouchings of esophageal mucosa can present with foul breath, regurgitation, and dysphagia. When present in the hypopharynx between the cricopharyngeus muscle and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle, they are termed a Zenker diverticulum. Barium swallow shows a posterior, midline outpouching above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus, which is not seen in this patient.

Choice D: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is incorrect. Early squamous carcinoma of the esophagus can cause dysphagia and weight loss. On endoscopy, early esophageal cancer can present as superficial plaques, nodules, or ulcerations. Advanced squamous cell carcinomas can present as strictures; large, ulcerated masses; or circumferential masses.

Apgar scores are 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Physical examination immediately after delivery shows a disproportionately large head compared with body size, a prominent forehead, depressed nasal bridge, and shortened upper arms and thighs. Muscle tone is decreased. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the growth hormone receptor. Which of the following sets of physiologic findings is most likely in this newborn?
  Growth Hormone Insulin-like
  Femur Length Secretion Growth Factor-1

Key Concept: Achondroplasia with a mutated growth hormone receptor will result in decreased IGF-1, decreased femur length, and increased growth hormone secretion.

A mutated growth hormone receptor will result in decreased ability to produce IGF-1. Additionally, due to decreased negative feedback, this will result in increased production of growth hormone.

Differential: A newborn with a growth hormone receptor mutation will present with short femur length, increased growth hormone secretion, and decreased IGF-1.

Choice A and Choice B are incorrect. Femur length will be decreased in the setting of abnormal growth hormone and IGF-1 signaling, not normal. This patient also has evidence of shortened upper arms and thighs on examination, consistent with decreased femur length.

questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of fever. Two months ago, she underwent a cadaveric kidney transplant for end-stage renal failure caused by polycystic kidney disease. Current medications include azathioprine, cyclosporine, and prednisolone. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Physical examination shows a well-healing surgical incision. Her serum creatinine concentration is 4.6 mg/dL compared with 1.1 mg/dL 1 day postoperatively. Microscopic examination of a renal biopsy specimen shows intimal swelling, endothelial hyperplasia, interstitial edema, and mononuclear cell infiltration. Antibodies directed against which of the following molecules are most likely to effectively treat the rejection episode in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Antibodies directed against CD3 are most likely to effectively treat this patient’s kidney transplant rejection.

Evaluation: Kidney transplant rejection should be suspected in patients presenting 2 months after transplant with fever, abnormal laboratory study results (eg, increased serum creatinine concentration), and acute kidney graft dysfunction, particularly when biopsy findings show mononuclear cell infiltration and endothelial injury.

Definition: Acute transplant rejection is mediated primarily by T lymphocytes that target donor antigens and initiate inflammatory damage to the graft. CD3 is a component of the T-lymphocyte receptor complex and is essential for T-lymphocyte activation. Without CD3, the pathophysiologic process of graft rejection would be interrupted.

Prevention: Immunosuppressive regimens, including calcineurin inhibitors, corticosteroids, and antimetabolites, are standard in preventing transplant rejection.

Treatment: Monoclonal antibodies are one component of the management of acute transplant rejection, along with corticosteroids and immunomodulators. Muromonab-CD3 is an example of a monoclonal antibody that targets CD3 for management of acute rejection.

Differential: Acute transplant rejection is mediated by T lymphocytes. Therefore, targeting CD3, an essential component of the T-lymphocyte receptor complex, is most likely to effectively treat the underlying pathophysiology of this patient’s kidney transplant rejection.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: B7 is incorrect. B7 proteins are ligands that regulate the immune response of host T lymphocytes, in this patient’s case, to antigens from donor grafts. B7 proteins can both activate or inhibit a T lymphocyte response, whereas CD3 is required for activation.

Choice C: IgE is incorrect. IgE is an immunoglobulin that is generally involved in type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions. IgE interacts with mast cells in this manner, not with T lymphocytes.

Choice D: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is incorrect. IL-1 is a cytokine that mediates fever and vascular inflammation among other functions. IL-1 is a nonspecific proinflammatory molecule and targeting it would not treat transplant rejection as effectively as targeting CD3.

Choice E: Tumor necrosis factor-α is incorrect. Tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitors are often used in the management of autoimmune diseases, such as Crohn disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and psoriasis.

questions.stemHtml: A 90-year-old man comes to the physician because of back pain and difficulty voiding for 1 month. He has arthritis treated with ibuprofen and hypertension treated with a diuretic. His blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows osteoarthritic changes in the hands and knees, a distended bladder, and an enlarged prostate gland. His hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 3.2 mg/dL. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows marked dilation of the renal pelves and ureters bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the increased serum creatinine concentration?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Age-associated decline in renal function

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Symptoms of an enlarged prostate gland include urinary dribbling and incontinence, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, nocturia, the need to frequently urinate, and incomplete voiding. The most likely cause of the increased serum creatinine concentration in this patient is due to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a possible cause of obstructive uropathy.

Evaluation: BPH affects middle-aged and older male patients and occurs due to excess growth of tissue in the central zone of the prostate causing lower urinary tract obstruction.

Definition: Symptoms are typically insidious in onset, chronic, and progressive. Chronic outlet obstruction leads to urinary retention and may cause the formation of bladder diverticulae or lead to hydronephrosis. Patients with urinary retention may develop urinary tract infections due to the loss of hydrodynamic flushing of bacteria out of the urethra. Diagnosis is made by history, physical, and urodynamic testing, along with ruling out alternate diagnoses (eg, prostatic malignancy).

Prevention: The development of hydronephrosis in this patient may have been prevented with treatment of his likely BPH.

Treatment: Treatment of BPH is with supportive care, α1-adrenergic blockers (eg, tamsulosin), and 5α-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride). Surgery may be indicated in refractory cases.

Differential: This 90-year-old patient with a 1-month history of voiding difficulty is found to have an enlarged prostate gland and hydronephrosis on ultrasonography. The resulting increased serum creatinine concentration is most consistent with obstructive uropathy, rather than intrinsic renal disease or age‑associated decline in renal function.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Age-associated decline in renal function is incorrect. This patient has a 1-month history of difficulty with voiding with findings of an enlarged prostate and hydronephrosis. Obstructive uropathy is the most likely cause of this patient’s increased serum creatinine concentration.

Choice B: Glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Glomerulonephritis refers to a variety of glomerular diseases, including nephritic and nephrotic syndromes. Nephritic syndromes typically present with acute renal failure with associated hematuria, red blood cell urine casts, and hypertension. Nephrotic syndrome typically presents with excessive proteinuria (greater than 3 g/day), hyperlipidemia, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. Glomerulonephritis would not typically cause obstructive uropathy.

Choice C: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is incorrect. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis refers to kidney damage that can occur in cases of chronic hypertension. Obstructive uropathy is the most likely cause of this patient’s increased serum creatinine concentration.

Choice E: Urate nephropathy is incorrect. Nephrolithiasis may present with colicky unilateral flank pain with radiation to the groin as well as associated hematuria. Nephrolithiasis may result in hydronephrosis but is more likely to cause unilateral rather than bilateral hydronephrosis.

  Alveolar Diffusing Pulmonary
  Transpulmonary Surface Capacity for Vascular
  Pressure Tension Carbon Monoxide Resistance

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Educational Objective: Newborns with an uncomplicated immediate neonatal transition, such as this patient, undergo normal cardiopulmonary adaptation immediately after birth, with lung expansion and oxygenation leading to decreased pulmonary vascular resistance and increased alveolar surface area for gas exchange. As a result, transpulmonary pressure increases, alveolar surface tension decreases, diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide increases, and pulmonary vascular resistance decreases.

Key Concept: At birth, the fetus switches from a placental source of gas exchange to using the lungs. This change is physiologically reflected by increased transpulmonary pressure, decreased alveolar surface tension, increased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance.

Explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is the difference between pressure in the alveoli and in the pleura. For normal gas exchange, there must be a difference in the pressures in these areas to create a driving force for air movement. Immediately after birth, such a pressure change occurs. Alveolar surface tension falls as amniotic fluid is absorbed and replaced with surfactant, which decreases surface tension permitting alveoli to remain patent for gas exchange. Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide increases, indicating that the relative thickness of the alveolar capillary interface has decreased as the lung expands. Finally, increased oxygen tension causes pulmonary vasodilation, which decreases pulmonary vascular resistance.

Differential: Based on this patient’s normal birth weight and reassuring Apgar scores, she is expected to undergo normal cardiopulmonary adaptation immediately after birth, resulting in pulmonary findings that include increased transpulmonary pressure and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, as well as decreased alveolar surface tension and pulmonary vascular resistance.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, E, and F.

Choices A, B, and D are incorrect. These options are incorrect because alveolar surface tension decreases due to the presence of surfactant after intrapleural amniotic fluid is absorbed, promoting alveolar expansion and increasing alveolar surface area for gas exchange.

Choices A, D, and E are incorrect. These options are incorrect because increased oxygenation after birth causes pulmonary vasodilation, decreasing pulmonary vascular resistance.

Choices D, E, and F are incorrect. These options are incorrect because transpulmonary pressure increases immediately after birth to generate a driving force for gas exchange. Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, a measure of effective gas exchange, also increases after birth.

questions.stemHtml: An investigator conducts a meta-analysis of three genome-wide association studies of type 1 diabetes mellitus. The studies assessed 7500 cases and 9000 reference samples. The meta-analysis identified an additional 20 risk loci. Ten of the loci (Group X) had odds ratios of 0.75 to 0.90 with confidence interval ranges of 0.70 to 0.95. The other 10 loci (Group Y) had odds ratios of 1.08 to 1.28 with confidence interval ranges of 1.02 to 1.41. Which of the following best explains the meta-analysis results?

options.label: A
options.html: A. The confidence intervals are too broad to permit interpretation of results

options.label: B
options.html: B. Group X loci are protective against the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus

options.label: C
options.html: C. The loci provide evidence for mendelian inheritance of type 1 diabetes mellitus

options.label: D
options.html: D. The majority of loci have major effects on the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus

options.label: E
options.html: E. Meta-analyses are only effective in determining loci with major effects on disease

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Odds ratios more than 1.0 with confidence intervals that do not contain 1.0 indicate that there is a higher likelihood of developing the disease when the risk factor is present, and odds ratios less than 1.0 with confidence intervals that do not contain 1.0 indicate that there is a lower likelihood of developing the disease when the risk factor is present. Therefore, the Group X loci are associated with a lower risk for developing type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Key Concept: Odds ratios with confidence intervals that do not contain 1.0 suggest a correlation between risk factor and disease.

Explanation: An odds ratio is the odds of an outcome in the group with the risk factor divided by the odds of the outcome in the group without the risk factor. Odds ratios are classically used in case-control studies and can assess associations between risk factors and diseases, particularly when the disease is rare. When relative statistical parameters are used, such as odds ratio or relative risk, 1.0 indicates there is no difference in disease risk between those with and without the proposed risk factor. Therefore, if the 95% confidence interval includes 1.0, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the risk factor is associated with the disease.

Differential: Because Group X loci had odds ratios and corresponding confidence intervals less than 1.0, these loci may have a protective effect against the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Confidence intervals being too broad is usually a critique when the association is nonsignificant. Inheritance patterns cannot be elicited from this study alone. Odds ratios can establish an association, but in isolation cannot indicate if the effects are major or minor.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: The confidence intervals are too broad to permit interpretation of results is incorrect. When power is too small to appreciate a statistically significant difference between two groups, this often leads to confidence intervals that are too broad. These confidence intervals are narrow and demonstrate statistical significance.

Choice C: The loci provide evidence for mendelian inheritance of type 1 diabetes mellitus is incorrect. This association study cannot determine what type of inheritance patterns dictate the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Choice D: The majority of loci have major effects on the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Odds ratios can establish an association but in isolation cannot indicate if the effects are major or minor.

Choice E: Meta-analyses are only effective in determining loci with major effects on disease is incorrect. Odds ratios can establish an association but in isolation cannot indicate if the effects are major or minor.

A 63-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He is lethargic. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are shown:
Serum

Additional laboratory testing is most likely to show an increased concentration of which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: In a patient with severe euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and increased urine sodium, additional laboratory testing is most likely to show an increased concentration of ADH (vasopressin). Rapid-onset or profound hyponatremia leads to cerebral edema and neurologic symptoms such as seizures, as seen in this patient.

Evaluation: This patient presents with seizure and lethargy in the setting of profound hyponatremia. Laboratory studies show decreased sodium with normal glucose, normal renal function, normal thyroid function, and adequate cortisol, excluding pseudohyponatremia, adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism. Urine is inappropriately concentrated with increased urine sodium despite hypotonic plasma, indicating impaired free water excretion rather than sodium depletion.

Definition: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion is characterized by nonphysiologic release of ADH leading to excessive water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. This causes dilutional hyponatremia with decreased serum osmolality while urine remains concentrated. Volume status is typically euvolemic because natriuresis counterbalances water retention. Neurologic symptoms such as seizures occur when hyponatremia develops rapidly or becomes severe.

Prevention: Prevention focuses on identifying and managing underlying causes such as medications, pulmonary disease, or central nervous system pathology.

Treatment: Acute symptomatic hyponatremia requires cautious correction with hypertonic saline and fluid restriction, with longer-term management directed at decreasing ADH effect.

Differential: Hypovolemic hyponatremia presents with decreased urine sodium and clinical volume depletion, while hypervolemic states show edema and increased brain-type natriuretic peptide. Endocrine causes of euvolemic hyponatremia are excluded by normal cortisol and thyroid studies.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, and D.

Choice B: B-type natriuretic peptide is incorrect. Brain-type natriuretic peptide is increased in hypervolemic states such as heart failure and promotes natriuresis, which is not the primary driver of water retention in euvolemic hyponatremia.

Choice C: Insulin is incorrect. Insulin regulates glucose uptake and potassium shifts and does not directly control renal water handling or urine concentration.

Choice D: Renin is incorrect. Renin is increased in hypovolemic states with decreased renal perfusion and leads to sodium and water retention rather than isolated water retention with natriuresis.

questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old nulligravid woman who has been unable to conceive for 4 years begins treatment with clomiphene. This treatment is most appropriate because it promotes ovulation through which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Activation of ovarian calcium channels

options.label: B
options.html: B. Direct stimulation of ovarian progesterone receptors

options.label: D
options.html: D. Inhibition of negative feedback by estrogen on follicle-stimulating hormone secretion

options.label: E
options.html: E. Stimulation of follicular growth factor receptors in the ovary

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Clomiphene is commonly used in the management of infertility, as in this case, to promote ovulation. Clomiphene induces ovulation by blocking estrogen-mediated negative feedback on the hypothalamus, increasing follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion.

Key Concept: Clomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, stimulates ovulation by blocking estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus.

Explanation: Clomiphene antagonizes estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, preventing estrogen from exerting negative feedback. This leads to increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone release from the hypothalamus and increased FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion from the pituitary, which leads to stimulation of follicular development and ovulation. Clomiphene is commonly used in anovulatory infertility, such as in polycystic ovary syndrome (now known as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome).

Differential: Increased FSH because of decreased estrogen negative feedback is the key mechanism underlying clomiphene-induced ovulation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Activation of ovarian calcium channels is incorrect. Activation of ovarian calcium channels is not the direct mechanism of clomiphene. Ovarian calcium channels play key roles in oocyte maturation and hormone production; however, their activation via clomiphene is indirect via downstream action of FSH and LH.

Choice B: Direct stimulation of ovarian progesterone receptors is incorrect. Progesterone receptors are not directly involved in the induction of ovulation, which is a function of FSH and LH.

Choice C: Inhibition of follistatin secretion is incorrect. Follistatin suppresses FSH release from the pituitary gland, whereas clomiphene acts at the hypothalamus. Clomiphene also acts at the estrogen receptor.

Choice E: Stimulation of follicular growth factor receptors in the ovary is incorrect. Clomiphene acts at the hypothalamus, not at the follicular growth factor receptor.

questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man dies in the hospital 3 days after he was admitted for appropriate treatment of complications of an anterior wall myocardial infarction. He had a history of coronary artery disease, aortic stenosis, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Medications were metformin, lisinopril, and albuterol. He had smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. A photograph of the patient’s heart, when cut from the left atrium to the left ventricle and exposing the mitral valve, is shown. Which of the following additional pathologic findings is most likely present at autopsy?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: This patient dies after anterior wall myocardial infarction, and autopsy shows papillary muscle rupture. The pathophysiology of hemodynamic collapse after papillary muscle rupture involves acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema.

Evaluation: Papillary muscle rupture classically presents 3 to 5 days after a transmural myocardial infarction with acute pulmonary edema that rapidly progresses to cardiogenic shock and potentially death. It results from necrosis of the papillary muscle and acute, severe mitral regurgitation.

Definition: Papillary muscle rupture occurs when myocardial infarction–induced ischemic necrosis, most often of the posteromedial papillary muscle supplied by a single coronary artery, weakens the tissue and causes acute rupture, resulting in sudden severe mitral regurgitation. The gold standard for diagnosis of papillary muscle rupture is with echocardiography or, as in this case, postmortem analysis.

Prevention: Papillary muscle rupture can be prevented by early reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction.

Treatment: Treatment for papillary muscle rupture includes emergency surgical mitral valve replacement and mechanical circulatory support to maintain hemodynamics.

Differential: This patient’s differential for cause of death is initially broad because he died after myocardial infarction. However, review of gross pathology shows papillary muscle rupture, which most likely led to pulmonary edema and hemodynamic collapse.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Cerebral embolism is incorrect. Cerebral embolism can result from atrial fibrillation or embolization of left ventricular thrombus but would not result from a papillary muscle rupture. Cerebral embolism would present with aphasia, hemiparesis, facial drooping, or other stroke-like symptoms.

Choice B: Constrictive pericarditis is incorrect. Constrictive pericarditis can result from radiation therapy but is not associated with papillary muscle rupture. Constrictive pericarditis presents with symptoms of heart failure, such as dyspnea on exertion, light-headedness, and edema.

Choice C: Hemopericardium is incorrect. Hemopericardium can result from free wall rupture, which is a possible mechanical complication of myocardial infarction. Free wall rupture is not seen in this photograph and is not this patient’s cause of death.

Choice E: Pulmonary embolism is incorrect. Pulmonary embolism presents with shortness of breath and tachycardia. It can cause hemodynamic collapse and death but is not a sequela of myocardial infarction or papillary muscle rupture.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe pain in his right thigh after falling 45 minutes ago. He has osteitis deformans (Paget disease) treated with intravenous bisphosphonate 6 months ago. An x-ray of the right lower extremity shows a transverse fracture of the femur 5 cm distal to the lesser trochanter with an anterior displacement of the proximal fragment. The unrestricted pull of which of the following muscles most likely produced the displacement of the proximal fragment in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Displacement of fracture fragments due to unrestricted muscle pulling can occur and is dependent on the origin and insertion of surrounding muscles. The iliopsoas flexes the hip and attaches at the lesser trochanter of the femur and, therefore, would be the most likely muscle to cause anterior displacement of the proximal fragment of a femur fracture distal to the lesser trochanter.

Key Concept: Anterior displacement of the proximal fragment of a femur fracture distal to the lesser trochanter can be due to the action of the iliopsoas.

Explanation: The resulting forces and movement of a limb is dependent on the actions and attachment sites of surrounding muscles. When a fracture occurs, bony fragments can move independently, and displacement may be affected by these surrounding muscles. The iliopsoas originates from the lumbar spine and iliac fossa and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur. The action of the iliopsoas as a hip flexor can result in anterior displacement of a proximal fracture fragment if the fracture is distal to the lesser trochanter.

Differential: The iliopsoas flexes the hip and attaches proximal to 5 cm distal to the lesser trochanter. The rectus femoris, sartorius, and vastus lateralis flex the hip, although they attach distal to the fracture. The adductor magnus adducts the hip and attaches distal to the fracture.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Adductor magnus is incorrect. Adductor magnus has a broad origination site along the inferior pelvis and inserts along the medial femur. The adductor magnus would medially displace the distal (not proximal) fracture fragment.

Choice C: Rectus femoris is incorrect. The rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and the superior acetabulum, inserting on the tibial tuberosity as part of the patellar ligament. The rectus femoris would not cause significant displacement of a hip fracture.

Choice D: Sartorius is incorrect. The sartorius originates from the anterior superior iliac spine, follows a diagonal course over the anterior thigh, and inserts in the medial tibia (pes anserinus). The sartorius would not cause significant displacement of a hip fracture.

Choice E: Vastus lateralis is incorrect. The vastus lateralis primarily originates from the greater trochanter of the femur and inserts on the tibial tuberosity as part of the patellar ligament. The vastus lateralis would not cause significant displacement of a hip fracture.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with hypertension is admitted to the hospital from the emergency department (ED) because of a 10-minute episode of nonexertional moderate chest pain and shortness of breath. In the ED, his serum troponin concentration was within the reference range, and an ECG showed nonspecific ST-T wave changes. On hospital day 1, the patient says he is anxious because he needs to "go home and get back to work." He is scheduled for echocardiography and cardiac catheterization tomorrow. The patient later asks the physician, "So what do you say, doc? Can I be discharged today and get the rest of my tests as an outpatient?" His medical chart shows that 6 months ago, he was scheduled for outpatient echocardiography and cardiac catheterization but did not keep his appointments or respond to attempts to schedule follow-up visits. Which of the following is the most appropriate physician response?

options.label: A
options.html: A. "Can you help me understand why it's so important for you to get back to work?"

options.label: B
options.html: B. "I understand this is very upsetting for you, but you must stay in the hospital until we finish evaluating you."

options.label: C
options.html: C. "I'm concerned you don't fully understand the gravity of your illness. Can you tell me more about your knowledge of coronary artery disease and heart attacks?"

options.label: D
options.html: D. "It would be much easier to get these tests done now than to worry about them as an outpatient. Why don't you stay a little longer until we get everything done, OK?"

options.label: E
options.html: E. "You didn't keep your previous appointments for these tests, so I’m concerned that you wouldn’t follow up again."

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: "Can you help me understand why it's so important for you to get back to work?" is the most appropriate physician response to this patient. When patients express concerns about a medical recommendation, physicians should initially explore their perspective to help build rapport and gather information to more effectively address the concerns.

Key Concept: When a patient expresses concern about a medical recommendation or requests to leave the hospital against medical advice, the physician should initially ask an open-ended, nonconfrontational question to explore that concern or request.

Explanation: Hearing the patient’s perspective will help build the patient-physician relationship and provide more information so that the physician can both validate the patient’s concern and target future discussion toward addressing the patient’s concern. For example, it is possible that the medical team would be able to assist this patient in being able to perform a particular work task remotely or in obtaining a letter excusing the patient from work duties. If the patient continues to request to discharge against medical advice, the physician should assess the patient’s decision-making capacity and consider discharging the patient with outpatient support.

Differential: Though physicians may be tempted to immediately provide education in an attempt to convince patients to change their mind, this approach may come across as judgment, potentially eliciting defensiveness, and is not as effective as first listening and exploring patients’ concerns.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: "I understand this is very upsetting for you, but you must stay in the hospital until we finish evaluating you” is incorrect. Telling the patient he must stay in the hospital opposes the patient’s agency in choosing whether to accept medical care.

Choice C: "I'm concerned you don't fully understand the gravity of your illness. Can you tell me more about your knowledge of coronary artery disease and heart attacks?" is inappropriate. This statement assumes a deficit within the patient rather than considering that the patient may have priorities that compete with remaining hospitalized. Before assessing the patient’s decision-making capacity or providing education, the physician should explore the reason for the patient’s request.

Choice D: "It would be much easier to get these tests done now than to worry about them as an outpatient. Why don't you stay a little longer until we get everything done, OK?" is inappropriate. It misses an opportunity to explore the patient’s perspective, build rapport, and more effectively address the patient’s concerns. It also opposes the patient’s agency in choosing whether to accept medical care.

Choice E: "You didn't keep your previous appointments for these tests, so I’m concerned that you wouldn’t follow up again” is incorrect. This statement may sound accusatory, and it misses an opportunity to understand the patient’s perspective. Later in the conversation, the physician could consider asking the patient about his barriers to outpatient follow-up with the goal of addressing those barriers.

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to the office with his girlfriend because she is concerned about how much alcohol he has been drinking during the past year. The patient says he does not have a problem. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He says he drinks four to six 12-oz beers and occasional liquor but only after work and on weekends. He adds that he is never intoxicated at work. There is a faint odor of alcohol on the patient's breath. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 88 kg (193 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2. Pulse is 103/min, and blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal obesity. On mental status examination, he has a depressed mood. Serum studies show an alkaline phosphatase activity of 160 U/L, ALT activity of 60 U/L, and γ-glutamyltransferase activity of 60 U/L (N=0–30). Which of the following factors is most consistent with the underlying diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Chronic alcohol use is commonly associated with increased serum γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) activity, which is a sensitive marker of alcohol-induced liver injury. Identifying biochemical markers helps support the diagnosis when patients underreport alcohol consumption.

Evaluation: Patients with alcohol use disorder may underreport their intake but present with subtle signs such as tachycardia, hypertension, and abnormal liver enzymes. Laboratory studies often show disproportionate increase of GGT activity and sometimes a greater AST than ALT activity, reflecting chronic alcohol exposure.

Definition: Alcohol use disorder is characterized by alcohol consumption leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, affecting generally more than one aspect of a patient’s life (eg, family, work). Chronic alcohol intake results in increased serum detection of hepatic enzymes, particularly GGT activities, which is a sensitive (though not specific) indicator of alcohol use. Other findings may include transaminase increases, often with AST greater than ALT activity, and evidence of metabolic complications. Patients may deny or underestimate their alcohol intake, making laboratory clues especially valuable. Early signs may include mood changes, autonomic symptoms, and subtle physical findings such as abdominal obesity.

Prevention: Prevention involves early screening and counseling on safe alcohol limits. Addressing risky drinking behaviors early can prevent progression to alcohol use disorder.

Treatment: Treatment includes behavioral therapy, support programs, and pharmacologic options such as naltrexone or acamprosate. Management of comorbid conditions and liver disease is important.

Differential: This patient has signs of chronic alcohol use despite denying excess intake. Increased GGT activity is a consistent laboratory finding supporting this diagnosis. The other factors listed are common to many other conditions and are not specific enough on their own to indicate excessive alcohol use.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Abdominal obesity is incorrect. Abdominal obesity is a risk factor for metabolic syndrome and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, but it is not specific for alcohol use. It does not directly indicate excessive alcohol consumption.

Choice B: Pulse is incorrect. Mild tachycardia can be seen in many conditions, including anxiety or early withdrawal, but it is nonspecific. Pulse does not confirm alcohol use.

Choice C: Serum alkaline phosphatase activity is not the best choice. Alkaline phosphatase is often increased in biliary disease such as cholelithiasis and cholangitis. It may be increased in alcohol use; however, it is nonspecific.

Choice D: Serum ALT activity is incorrect. ALT activity above normal indicates hepatocellular injury but is not specific to alcohol and is often higher in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease or viral hepatitis. Alcohol-related liver injury more commonly shows AST activity predominance.

questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has asthma. He is most likely to be treated effectively with a bronchodilator that increases the concentration of which of the following second messengers in the smooth muscle cells of his bronchi?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction caused by airway smooth-muscle contraction. β2-Adrenergic agonists relieve bronchospasm by increasing intracellular cAMP in bronchial smooth muscle cells, leading to relaxation and bronchodilation.

Key Concept: cAMP acts as a second messenger in smooth muscle cells to activate protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and inhibits myosin light-chain kinase, decreasing actin–myosin interactions and causing muscle relaxation. β2-Adrenergic agonists, such as albuterol, use this pathway to reverse airway constriction in asthma.

Explanation: This younger patient with asthma may experience acute bronchospasm, presenting as shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. β2-Adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle are Gs protein–coupled, and stimulation increases adenylate cyclase, which increases cAMP concentrations. Increased cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates targets that decreases intracellular calcium and inhibits myosin light-chain phosphorylation. This biochemical pathway causes smooth-muscle relaxation and relief of airway obstruction. Short-acting β2-adrenergic agonists are the mainstay for acute asthma exacerbations. Long-acting β2-adrenergic agonists are used in combination with inhaled corticosteroids for maintenance therapy of persistent asthma.

Differential: Bronchodilation in asthma is achieved by increasing cAMP, distinguishing β2-adrenergic agonists from drugs that act via cGMP, calcium, or other second messengers. Rapid symptom relief depends on smooth-muscle relaxation rather than anti-inflammatory effects.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F.

Choice A and Choice E: Calcium and inositol triphosphate are incorrect. Increased intracellular calcium promotes smooth-muscle contraction, not relaxation. Increasing intracellular calcium would have the opposite effect, worsening bronchoconstriction. Inositol triphosphate leads to release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Choice C and Choice F: cGMP and nitric oxide are incorrect. cGMP mediates relaxation in vascular smooth muscle in response to nitric oxide, but it is not the primary mediator in bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors act to prolong the action of nitric oxide within the cGMP pathway, leading to vasodilation primarily in pulmonary, nasal, and genital vascular beds. While nitric oxide increases cGMP and causes vascular smooth-muscle relaxation, this occurs in vasculature, not in the bronchial smooth muscle.

Choice D: Diacylglycerol is incorrect. Diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C and typically promotes smooth-muscle contraction, not relaxation.

questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. Physical examination shows a 5-cm right-sided abdominal mass. Renal ultrasonography shows a right kidney mass. A right nephrectomy is done and pathology confirms the diagnosis of nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor). Gene expression studies are done on the tumor tissue and a sample of the patient's normal tissue. These studies indicate that the normal tissue has one active allele for the insulin-like growth factor 2 gene (IGF2) and the tumor tissue has two active IGF2 alleles. Which of the following best explains the observed gene dosage results?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Growth factor alleles are expressed equally unless a mutation is present

options.label: B
options.html: B. Loss of normal imprinting occurred as part of carcinogenesis in the tumor tissue

options.label: C
options.html: C. Paternal imprinting is present in the normal tissue and maternal imprinting in the tumor

options.label: D
options.html: D. The patient is heterozygous for a loss-of-function mutation in the IGF2 allele

options.label: E
options.html: E. Tumor tissue developed a mutation that caused imprinting of the IGF2 allele

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: This 4-year-old boy has been identified to have a nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) with two active IGF2 alleles identified on gene expression studies of the tumor tissue. Loss of normal imprinting most likely occurred as part of the carcinogenesis of the tumor tissue.

Key Concept: A nephroblastoma is a malignant renal tumor found in children. It is commonly asymptomatic and found on physical examination with identification of a palpable unilateral renal mass.

Explanation: Nephroblastoma is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which occurs as a result of inappropriate imprinting of one or more genes. Imprinting refers to suppression of either the maternal or paternal allele for a particular gene leading to monoallelic expression of that gene. Imprinting may occur by methylation of DNA or modification of histone proteins, and results in underexpression or complete repression of the affected allele. IGF2 normally undergoes genomic imprinting with only the paternally inherited allele being active.

Differential: This patient has two active IGF2 alleles in the nephroblastoma tissue. The loss of normal imprinting occurring as part of carcinogenesis in the tumor tissue best explains the observed gene dosage result.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Growth factor alleles are expressed equally unless a mutation is present is incorrect. Normally, the maternal IGF2 allele is silenced. Loss of normal imprinting is the more likely explanation.

Choice C: Paternal imprinting is present in the normal tissue and maternal imprinting in the tumor is incorrect. This patient was found to have a single active allele in the normal tissue and two active alleles in the tumor tissue. The tumor tissue with two active IGF2 alleles indicates there was a loss of normal imprinting.

Choice D: The patient is heterozygous for a loss-of-function mutation in the IGF2 allele is incorrect. The tumor tissue was identified to have two active alleles indicating a loss of normal imprinting. Normal tissue has silencing of the maternal IGF2 allele.

Choice E: Tumor tissue developed a mutation that caused imprinting of the IGF2 allele is incorrect. Normal tissue has imprinting of the IGF2 allele with the paternal allele active. This patient’s tumor tissue had a loss of imprinting, which is indicated by two active alleles.

questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of watery diarrhea. Her respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show achlorhydria and hypokalemia. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a 3-cm mass in the pancreas. Immunohistochemical labeling of neoplastic cells in a biopsy specimen is most likely to involve the use of antibodies directed to which of the following pancreatic proteins?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: H.

Educational Objective: This patient’s presentation including profuse watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, and a pancreatic mass is consistent with a vipoma due to excess vasoactive intestinal polypeptide secretion.

Evaluation: This patient presents with 2 weeks of large-volume watery diarrhea accompanied by tachypnea and electrolyte abnormalities, specifically hypokalemia. Laboratory evidence of achlorhydria indicates suppression of gastric acid secretion rather than inflammatory or infectious diarrhea. Imaging identifies a pancreatic mass, localizing the source to an endocrine pancreatic tumor rather than a primary gastrointestinal process.

Definition: Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) can be produced by vipomas, rare neuroendocrine tumors of the pancreas that arise from non-beta islet cells. Vipoma syndrome, also called Verner-Morrison syndrome, results from inappropriate VIP secretion by a neuroendocrine tumor and leads to increased secretion of water and electrolytes by the intestines while inhibiting gastric acid secretion, as well as the increased relaxation of smooth muscle fibers in the gastrointestinal tract. This results in profound fluid and electrolyte secretion into the gastrointestinal tract, severe watery diarrhea, electrolyte disturbances, achlorhydria, hypokalemic metabolic acidosis, flushing, and vasodilation. This leads to watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria, which is collectively referred to as WDHA syndrome. Persistent fluid loss can cause dehydration and metabolic disturbances.

Prevention: There is no established prevention, but early recognition limits complications from severe electrolyte and volume depletion.

Treatment: Management includes aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement and somatostatin analogs to decrease VIP secretion, along with surgery and/or chemotherapy.

Differential: Secretory diarrheas from endocrine tumors are distinguished from malabsorptive or inflammatory causes by persistence during fasting and associated hormonal effects such as achlorhydria.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.

Choice A: Amylase is incorrect. Amylase is produced by pancreatic acinar cells and is involved in carbohydrate digestion, not secretory diarrhea or electrolyte abnormalities.

Choice B: Gastrin is incorrect. Gastrin-secreting tumors cause hyperchlorhydria and peptic ulcer disease rather than achlorhydria with watery diarrhea.

Choice C: Glucagon is incorrect. Glucagonomas cause diabetes mellitus, weight loss, and necrolytic migratory erythema, not profuse watery diarrhea.

Choice D: Human pancreatic polypeptide is incorrect. Pancreatic polypeptide–secreting tumors are often clinically silent and do not produce severe diarrhea or hypokalemia.

Choice E: Insulin is incorrect. Insulinomas cause hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenic symptoms rather than secretory diarrhea.

Choice F: Lipase is incorrect. Lipase is an exocrine enzyme involved in fat digestion and is not associated with endocrine tumor syndromes.

Choice G: Serotonin is incorrect. Serotonin-secreting tumors cause carcinoid syndrome with flushing, bronchospasm, and diarrhea, typically arising from the small intestine rather than the pancreas.

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-day history of a red lesion on his left leg. He recently returned from a 1-year missionary trip to Brazil. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photographs. Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen of the lesion shows 2- to 4-μm, round organisms within macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely vector of this patient’s infection?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 4-day history of an ulcerated lesion following an extended trip to Brazil, and intracellular organisms on microscopy suggestive of leishmaniasis infection. The most likely vector of this patient’s infection is the sand fly.

Evaluation: Leishmaniasis may present with several clinical variants, including a cutaneous form. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is often characterized by solitary or sparse, ulcerated and crateriform, friable plaques. Lesions at the site of the sand fly bite are generally painless, although pain may occur if complications such as secondary infection develop. Biopsy may show intracellular amastigotes within macrophages under microscopy. Molecular polymerase chain reaction from affected tissue can determine the subtype of Leishmania species.

Definition: Leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection transmitted to humans via sand fly bite. Individual Leishmania species will affect the clinical presentation of disease.

Prevention: Patients living or traveling to endemic areas may use diethyltoluamide insect repellent to prevent sand fly bites.

Treatment: Cutaneous leishmaniasis may self-resolve with residual scarring, but if diagnosed in a timely manner, can be treated with pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate. Systemic and severe forms of leishmaniasis are typically treated with amphotericin B.

Differential: This patient’s ulcerated skin lesion following prolonged travel to an endemic region, together with biopsy demonstrating intracellular amastigotes within macrophages, is most consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis transmitted by sand fly bite.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Flea is incorrect. Fleas are commonly a vector for rickettsial infections, which cause endemic typhus. Typhus is associated with the development of fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. Treatment of typhus includes oral tetracyclines, including doxycycline.

Choice B: Louse is incorrect. Common conditions associated with lice infections include head lice, body lice, and pubic lice. These are all caused by members of the Pediculus humanas species. Lice infections are associated with close contact with affected individuals and treatment includes topical permethrin.

Choice C: Mosquito is incorrect. Mosquitos are the vectors of multiple infections, including West Nile virus, eastern equine encephalitis, and filariasis. Mosquitos are not the causative vector for leishmaniasis.

Choice E: Tick is incorrect. Ticks represent the vectors for Lyme disease. Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and initially presents with the erythema migrans rash. Lyme disease is commonly treated with tetracycline antibiotics, including doxycycline.

questions.stemHtml: A 5-month-old girl is brought to the office because of a 2-week history of episodes of severe cough that frequently lead to vomiting. The patient had an upper respiratory tract illness for several days prior to the onset of coughing. Her 4-year-old sister had similar symptoms earlier this month, and her caregiver has had a mild, hacking cough for more than 1 month. She appears well. Physical examination and chest x-ray show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: This patient, with paroxysmal coughing followed by post-tussive vomiting, most likely has pertussis, which often presents in infants without fever or abnormal lung examination findings.

Evaluation: This patient has a classic history for pertussis: a preceding upper respiratory illness followed by weeks of severe coughing spells. The absence of fever, normal physical examination, normal chest x-ray, and exposure to family members with prolonged cough further support this diagnosis.

Definition: Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, a gram-negative coccobacillus that produces pertussis toxin. Pertussis progresses through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, with the paroxysmal stage characterized by episodic coughing fits and post-tussive vomiting, as in this patient. Infants can also present with apnea, cyanosis, or vomiting. Vaccinated adolescents and adults may develop a mild but prolonged cough and serve as reservoirs of infection. Infants younger than 6 months, who have not yet completed the primary diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine series, are at highest risk for severe disease and complications.

Prevention: Pertussis is preventable through routine childhood immunization and booster vaccination in adolescents, adults, and pregnant individuals. Vaccinating close contacts helps protect vulnerable infants.

Treatment: Treatment consists of macrolide antibiotics, such as azithromycin, which decrease transmission and may lessen disease severity if administered early.

Differential: This patient’s age, post-tussive vomiting, lack of fever, and exposure to close contacts with chronic cough most strongly suggests pertussis over other respiratory infections. The other potential diagnoses listed typically present with fever and/or abnormal lung examination findings, which this patient does not have.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Diphtheria is incorrect. Diphtheria typically presents with sore throat, fever, and a gray pseudomembrane on the tonsils or pharynx, not isolated paroxysmal coughing with vomiting. This patient does not have fever or an abnormal physical examination.

Choice B: Influenza A is incorrect. Influenza usually causes acute fever, myalgias, and systemic symptoms rather than a prolonged, paroxysmal cough without fever.

Choice C: Measles is incorrect. Measles presents with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a characteristic rash, none of which are present in this patient.

Choice D: Metapneumovirus infection is incorrect. Human metapneumovirus commonly causes bronchiolitis or pneumonia with wheezing and abnormal lung findings, which are absent in this patient.

questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of difficulty eating and speaking for 4 days. When he is asked to protrude his tongue, it deviates to the left side. His taste sensation is normal. Which of the following nerves has most likely been injured?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with a left-sided tongue deviation without alteration of his taste sensation. This is most likely the result of a left hypoglossal nerve injury.

Key Concept: Hypoglossal nerve injury may present with ipsilateral tongue deviation, dysarthria, dysphagia, and tongue atrophy.

Explanation: The hypoglossal nerve innervates the intrinsic and the majority of the extrinsic tongue muscles. Hypoglossal nerve injury may occur due to a variety of reasons including postoperative injury, neoplastic disease, or idiopathic causes. Recovery of the nerve is dependent on the underlying cause and degree of impairment. Treatment often is initially conservative with speech therapy.

Differential: This patient presents with dysphagia, dysarthria, and left-sided tongue deviation without a loss of taste. Left-sided tongue deviation occurs in this case because of unopposed action of the functioning right-sided tongue muscles.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Left glossopharyngeal is incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve is responsible for motor innervation of the stylopharyngeus muscle, sensation to the pharynx and carotid body, and the sense of taste along the posterior third of the tongue. The findings in this case are more indicative of a left hypoglossal nerve injury.

Choice C and Choice E: Left lingual and right lingual are incorrect. The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. The lingual nerve provides sensation to the floor of the mouth as well as taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue. The findings in this case are more indicative of a left hypoglossal nerve injury.

Choice D: Right hypoglossal is incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve is a pure motor nerve that provides innervation to the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue. Injury to the right hypoglossal nerve would result in a right-sided tongue deviation.

questions.stemHtml: A 2-week-old female newborn is brought to the emergency department by her mother because of a 2-day history of nasal congestion. The mother recently emigrated from Guatemala, and she does not speak English. The mother is accompanied by her 6-year-old niece who speaks English. A hospital interpreter is currently busy but estimates that she could be available in approximately 1 hour. Both a male and female janitor in the emergency department speak Spanish. The physician speaks only a few words of Spanish. The patient's temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 40/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate method for the physician to obtain a medical history for this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Try to communicate in Spanish without an interpreter

options.label: B
options.html: B. Use the female janitor as the interpreter

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: For patients who do not speak the dominant language of a hospital system, informed consent should be facilitated by a trained interpreter. The most appropriate method for the physician to obtain this patient’s medical history is to wait for the hospital interpreter.

Key Concept: Professional interpreters can provide high-quality translations that maintain patient safety.

Explanation: Credentialed interpreters are trained in medical knowledge and vocabulary, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. Relying on a family member or other hospital staff to interpret for the patient increases the risk for miscommunication about medical or culturally relevant information. This can jeopardize informed consent for treatment and patient safety.

Differential: Circumventing an interpreter should only be considered if a procedure is emergent (eg, the patient will imminently lose their life or a limb) and an interpreter is unavailable.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choices A, B, C, and D: Try to communicate in Spanish without an interpreter, use the female janitor as the interpreter, use the male janitor as the interpreter, and use the 6-year-old girl as the interpreter are incorrect. These strategies are all more likely to result in miscommunications than the use of a professional interpreter.

questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of progressive muscle weakness. He recently received the diagnosis of small cell lung carcinoma. Neurologic examination shows symmetric weakness of the proximal upper and lower extremity muscles, which transiently improves with exercise. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in all extremities. Laboratory studies show antibodies directed against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these clinical findings?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 2-month history of progressive muscle weakness and a recent diagnosis of small cell lung carcinoma. He is found to have weakness that improves with exercise, which is consistent with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). LEMS is a disorder that results in impaired acetylcholine release.

Key Concept: LEMS classically presents with weakness in the proximal muscles that transiently improves with repeated muscle contraction. It results from autoantibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels.

Explanation: In LEMS, destruction of voltage gated calcium channels decreases calcium influx into presynaptic nerve terminals, thereby preventing the release of acetylcholine. The gold standard for diagnosis is based on clinical features, electrophysiologic studies, and anti–voltage-gated calcium channel antibody serology. LEMS cannot be prevented as it is an autoimmune disorder. However, it is often associated with small cell lung carcinoma, which can be prevented by minimizing oncologic risk and improving lifestyle habits.

Differential: This patient’s differential is initially broad when he presents with muscle weakness. However, it is quickly narrowed with his diagnosis of small cell lung carcinoma, his symmetric weakness that improves with exercise, and his antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, which are consistent with LEMS, which impairs acetylcholine release.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Desensitization of nicotinic receptors is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic disorder where antibodies decrease nicotinic receptor function. Myasthenia gravis often presents with fatigable weakness, while this patient has weakness that improves with exercise.

Choice C: Impaired actin-myosin interaction is incorrect. Some congenital myopathies result from impaired actin-myosin interaction; however, such myopathies would present chronically. This patient has LEMS.

Choice D: Impaired excitation-contraction coupling is incorrect. Impaired excitation-contraction coupling classically occurs in heart failure where the myocytes are unable to contract when they are excited by the cardiac electrical system.

Choice E: Motor nerve conduction block is incorrect. Motor nerve conduction blocks occur in immune-mediated neuropathies such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and present as progressive weakness.
